definition: The Roman spa town of Bath in Somerset, where bathers dropped over 130 scratched lead curse tablets into Sulis Minerva’s hot spring.
Travelling royal courts set up by King Henry II where royal judges rode round English counties to hear serious cases before local juries.
Nickname for harsh 18th-century British laws that punished over 220 crimes—even stealing five shillings or chopping down trees—by hanging.
Popular nickname (alongside "Peelers") for London’s first uniformed Metropolitan Police officers, named after founder Sir Robert Peel in 1829.
One shared royal law for all England introduced under King Henry II, replacing patchwork local customs with consistent judge and jury rules.
A thin folded sheet of Roman lead (defixio) scratched with Latin letters begging a god or goddess to track down and punish an unknown thief.
Designing harsh or public punishments—like village stocks or treason executions—to frighten onlookers so nobody dares copy the crime.
Genetic forensic test discovered in 1984 by Professor Sir Alec Jeffreys in Leicester, matching unique DNA from tiny traces of blood, hair, or saliva.
A wooden chair fixed to the end of a long see-saw beam used in Tudor and Stuart towns to dunk accused scolds or dishonest bakers into cold river water.
Unique patterns of loops, arches, and whorls on human fingertips, adopted by London’s Scotland Yard Fingerprint Bureau in 1901 to solve crimes.
Strict Norman laws created by William the Conqueror after 1066 banning ordinary villagers from hunting wild deer or cutting wood in royal forests.
Scientific crime-solving methods—including fingerprints, microscope fibres, ballistics, and DNA—used to prove guilt or clear innocent suspects.
Betraying or plotting to kill the monarch or blow up Parliament—such as the 1605 Gunpowder Plot—treated as the most serious crime in Britain.
An armed robber on horseback in the 1700s—like Dick Turpin—who held up slow stagecoaches along unlit roads with flintlock pistols.
An Anglo-Saxon and medieval alarm shouted or blown on a horn requiring every villager within earshot to stop work and chase a suspect at once.
A group of twelve sworn citizens who listen carefully to courtroom evidence and witnesses before deciding fairly whether a suspect is guilty or innocent.
A Roman or modern local judge who hears court cases, weighs witness statements, and decides lawful fines or sentences.
The "Great Charter" sealed by King John at Runnymede in 1215, promising that even the king must obey the law and free citizens deserve a fair trial.
An upright wooden frame on a market-square post with holes locking an offender’s head and wrists while village crowds watched.
Secretly hunting deer, rabbits, or pheasants on royal or landowner estates—seen by many hungry villagers as a "social crime".
An old dismasted wooden warship moored on rivers like the Thames to hold overcrowded convicts in damp chains before transportation.
Helping offenders change their lives for good through clean prisons, schooling, and work skills—championed at Newgate by Elizabeth Fry.
Medieval Church protection lasting up to 37–40 days for any fugitive who struck a cathedral door knocker, pausing arrest before trial or exile.
Secretly landing untaxed goods like tea, silk, and brandy onto dark beaches at night to dodge heavy 18th-century government customs taxes.
An Anglo-Saxon group of ten local males aged twelve and over who promised to keep one another honest or bring lawbreakers to court.
Sending over 160,000 convicted British prisoners by ship between 1787 and 1868 to serve hard-labour sentences in Australian colonies.
An Anglo-Saxon and early medieval church test—using red-hot iron or cold water—asking God to show guilt or innocence when witnesses could not agree.
Old English for "person-price"—a fixed sum of silver coins paid by a wrongdoer’s family to an injured victim’s kin to stop violent blood feuds.
